stories.headline: Denver Pedestrian Seriously Injured in Hit-and-Run Near Chaffee Park
stories.summary:
A pedestrian was struck and seriously injured by a hit-and-run driver near 48th Avenue and Kalamath Street in Denver's Chaffee Park neighborhood at approximately 1:48 a.m. Saturday, according to the Denver Police Department. Authorities issued a Medina Alert seeking the public's help identifying the vehicle and driver.

The suspect vehicle is described as a 2003-2007 Chevrolet Silverado with Colorado license plates, featuring a gray cab, black truck bed, blue tailgate and mismatched wheels on the driver's side. The driver is believed to be a white or Hispanic male between 25 and 30 years old with dark hair.

The Colorado Bureau of Investigation shared the alert on social media to aid in the search. Anyone with information is asked to call 911 or the Denver Police Department at 720-913-2000.

stories.headline: Man Accused of Vandalism Spree Spanning Aurora, Denver and Douglas County
stories.summary:
A 42-year-old man, Worku Woldemariam, has been accused of a string of vandalism incidents across the Denver metro area spanning several weeks, according to court records and witness accounts. Alleged incidents include cutting down American and Colorado flags outside the Douglas County Sheriff's Office substation, smashing artwork at an Aurora market, throwing a rock through a King Soopers Starbucks window and destroying an urban community garden in Aurora.

Despite multiple contacts with law enforcement, Woldemariam was released on bond after a Douglas County arrest and continued to allegedly commit acts of destruction. The owner of Nugg's Ice Cream on Colfax said a man matching Woldemariam's description threw rocks through the shop's windows, though Denver police said no arrests have been made in that case.

The urban garden targeted on E. 16th Avenue in Aurora serves refugees from multiple countries who rely on it for food. Garden manager Matthew King said Woldemariam destroyed a water tank, defaced the property for hours and threatened a gardener's husband with a rock and stick. The case has drawn concern from community members and business owners about the pace of law enforcement response.

stories.headline: Denver Moves to Shut Down Five Points Nightclub After Security Guard Accused of Sexual Assault at Gunpoint
stories.summary:
The City of Denver is moving to shut down a Five Points nightclub following allegations that a security guard sexually assaulted a patron at gunpoint on the premises. The action reflects the city's authority to revoke business licenses from establishments where serious crimes occur.

Details of the specific incident, including the name of the nightclub and the identity of the accused security guard, were part of the city's enforcement action. Sexual assault at gunpoint is a serious felony offense under Colorado law.

The move signals Denver's continued use of licensing enforcement as a public safety tool against establishments linked to violent or predatory criminal conduct. The nightclub's operators would have recourse to contest the closure through city administrative proceedings.

stories.headline: After Ranked-Choice Voting Defeat, New Colorado Group Prepares Fresh Push for Election Reform
stories.summary:
A new organization called Courageous Colorado, assembled largely from veterans of the failed 2024 Proposition 131 campaign, is laying the groundwork for a multi-year effort to overhaul how Colorado elections are conducted. The group's agenda includes supporting ranked-choice voting in Longmont, expanding the Boulder County commission, potentially changing when municipal elections are held and reforming how candidates qualify for the ballot.

Ultimately, the group expects to pursue ballot measures related to Colorado's partisan primaries, potentially seeking to replace them with an open primary system similar to California's, where all candidates appear on a single ballot regardless of party. CEO Landon Mascareñaz said voters should expect legislative and ballot activity around open primaries, ranked-choice voting and campaign finance reform over the coming election cycles.

The group's bipartisan supporters include former Democratic House Speaker Terrance Carroll, former Republican state GOP chairman Dick Wadhams and Democratic Socialists of America member Deep Singh Badhesha. Proposition 131, which would have opened primaries and instituted ranked-choice voting in general elections, lost by nearly seven percentage points in 2024. Organizers argue reforms are needed in part because Colorado's Democratic lean means many races are effectively decided in June primaries, in which unaffiliated voters — now more than 50 percent of registered voters — can only participate in one party's contest.

stories.headline: Federal Judge Says 'Smoking-Gun' Email Links Trump Administration to Retaliation Against Colorado
stories.summary:
A federal judge has found that a so-called smoking-gun email directly links the Trump administration to retaliation against Colorado, according to reporting from the Denver Gazette. The ruling marks a significant development in a legal dispute between the state and federal government.

The specific nature of the retaliation and the underlying dispute were detailed in court proceedings. Colorado has been engaged in several high-profile conflicts with the Trump administration over immigration enforcement, federal funding and other policy areas.

The judge's language about a smoking-gun document suggests the evidence could be highly damaging to the federal government's position in the case. The ruling's outcome could have significant implications for Colorado's ongoing legal battles with the administration.

stories.headline: Colorado AG Sues GEO Group Over Refusal to Comply with Tuberculosis Investigation at Aurora ICE Facility
stories.summary:
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser has filed a lawsuit against the GEO Group, the private prison company that operates the Aurora immigration detention center, over the company's refusal to cooperate with a state tuberculosis investigation at the facility. The lawsuit represents an escalation of the state's efforts to exercise public health oversight at the detention center.

The dispute reflects ongoing tension between Colorado state authorities and the operators of the Aurora facility, which houses federal immigration detainees. A federal judge had previously blocked a state law requiring regular inspections of the center, a ruling reported in this digest earlier this week.

Tuberculosis is a communicable disease subject to mandatory public health reporting and investigation under state law. The AG's office argues GEO Group's noncompliance poses a risk to detainees, staff and the broader community. GEO Group has not publicly commented on the lawsuit's specifics.

stories.headline: Infleqtion Opens 80,000-Square-Foot Colorado Quantum Innovation Center in Louisville as Company Reaches $3 Billion Valuation
stories.summary:
Infleqtion, a quantum technology company, has opened an 80,000-square-foot Colorado Quantum Innovation Center in Louisville, marking a major expansion of quantum computing and sensing research infrastructure along the Front Range. The company has reached a $3 billion valuation, reflecting growing investor confidence in the emerging quantum technology sector.

The facility is expected to serve as a hub for research, development and commercialization of quantum technologies, which have potential applications in computing, sensing, communications and national security. Colorado has emerged as a national center for quantum research, with significant activity at the University of Colorado Boulder, the National Institute of Standards and Technology and a cluster of private companies.

The opening represents a significant economic development win for Louisville and Boulder County. Quantum technology companies have been among the most closely watched startups in the state as the sector matures from basic research toward commercial products.

stories.headline: Colorado Job Growth Slows, but Some Employers Continue Hiring Amid Economic Uncertainty
stories.summary:
Colorado employers added an estimated 5,800 jobs in July, according to the state labor department's latest report, continuing a pattern of slower-than-expected job growth that has prompted economists at the University of Colorado's Business Research Division to cut their 2027 job growth forecasts by more than half. June's preliminary job figures were also revised downward, a pattern repeated throughout the year.

Despite sluggish headline numbers, some Colorado employers are actively expanding. Aerospace company Ursa Major opened a new rocket-motor manufacturing plant in Longmont, choosing to expand in Colorado with the help of up to $35.3 million in state tax credits tied to adding 1,850 jobs over eight years. The Berthoud-based company currently employs 300 people in Colorado and has 120 open positions.

Lakewood-based Terumo Blood and Cell Technologies, a medical products manufacturer, is using a long-running internship program to fill positions, hiring 62.5 percent of its intern cohort last year. The company has more than 60 open positions in Colorado. Economists note that while job growth has muted, state GDP and income continue to grow, suggesting productivity gains are offsetting some of the employment slowdown.

stories.headline: Bear Attacks Fisherman on Jefferson County Trail; Wildlife Officials Euthanize Animal
stories.summary:
A bear attacked and injured a fisherman on the North Fork Trail in Jefferson County on Friday evening, marking the sixth bear attack in Colorado so far in 2026 — double the number recorded in all of 2025. The attack occurred around 8 p.m. as the man, who is in his 60s, was walking back to a parking lot after fishing near the confluence of the Platte rivers.

The bear, described as a subadult sow, knocked the man to the ground and bit his legs in an attack that lasted several minutes before the victim's friends scared the animal away. The man was hospitalized with injuries described as not life-threatening.

Colorado Parks and Wildlife officers and a U.S. Department of Agriculture dog team tracked and euthanized the bear early Saturday morning. CPW officials said the animal showed no signs of nursing and no cubs were found nearby. Officials attributed the increase in bear activity and conflicts this year to historic drought conditions that have reduced the animals' natural food sources, pushing them closer to populated areas during their hyperphagia phase, when bears consume up to 20,000 calories per day to prepare for hibernation.

stories.headline: Waymo Driverless Robotaxis Set to Launch in Denver Later This Year
stories.summary:
Waymo, the autonomous vehicle subsidiary of Alphabet, has announced plans to launch driverless robotaxi service in Denver later this year, marking a significant expansion of the company's commercial operations beyond its current markets in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Phoenix. The announcement positions Denver among a small number of U.S. cities with access to fully autonomous ride-hailing services.

The launch would make Denver the first major Colorado city to host a commercial robotaxi service, representing a milestone for the region's transportation landscape. Waymo vehicles operate without a human safety driver and use a combination of cameras, radar and lidar sensors to navigate city streets.

The rollout is expected to generate significant public interest and regulatory attention. Denver city officials and the Colorado Department of Transportation have been monitoring autonomous vehicle development as part of broader transportation planning efforts.

stories.headline: Broncos Fall to Packers 33-10 in Home Preseason Game; Nix Solid in Return from Injury
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos lost to the Green Bay Packers 33-10 on Friday night at Empower Field, ending the team's eight-game preseason winning streak. The lopsided result prompted a pointed postgame assessment from head coach Sean Payton, who said he could not identify a single phase in which Denver played even with or outperformed Green Bay.

Quarterback Bo Nix, returning to game action for the first time in seven months following an ankle injury, was a bright spot, completing 6 of 9 passes for 76 yards and a touchdown. The Broncos scored on their first two possessions behind Nix before the offense stalled. Backup Jarrett Stidham threw an interception, Denver committed 10 penalties and the Packers scored on seven of their nine possessions.

Payton declined to confirm whether Nix and other starters would play in Denver's preseason finale against Minnesota, though he initially said he wanted starters to play into the third quarter before acknowledging cooler heads would likely prevail. The Broncos must finalize their 53-man roster by Aug. 30 before opening the regular season against the Kansas City Chiefs. Undrafted wide receiver Kolbe Katsis generated notice with four kickoff returns for 117 yards, while seventh-round pick Khalil Murdock leads the team with 16 preseason tackles.

stories.headline: Jason Richardson Joins Altitude Sports as Nuggets Analyst, Explaining His Deep Denver Ties
stories.summary:
Altitude Sports has added former NBA guard Jason Richardson to its revamped Denver Nuggets broadcast team, a choice that has drawn some scrutiny given that Richardson never played for the Nuggets during his 14-year professional career. Richardson addressed the skepticism directly, explaining that his connection to Denver dates to 2002 or 2003, when he began dating his future wife Jackie Paul, a former Boulder High School and UCCS athlete.

Richardson said the couple spent off-seasons in Colorado throughout his playing career, and that his daughter graduated from Cherry Creek High School while his sons attended Colorado Academy. He described Denver as home for his family and said he and his wife decided to return to the city as empty nesters after their sons left to pursue their own basketball careers.

Altitude Sports announced the new broadcast lineup this week. Richardson's son Jase is entering his second NBA season with the Orlando Magic, having been selected with the Denver pick included in the Aaron Gordon trade. Richardson's other son Jaxon, a five-star recruit, recently enrolled at the University of Alabama. Richardson, 45, said he credits broadcaster Vic Lombardi with helping connect him with Altitude's leadership.
